title: Lesson Desk (All of a Sutton)
oneLine: Turns one sentence from a teacher into a full textbook-grounded lesson: slides, group activity, worksheet and answer key, in about five minutes.

specs.Model: Claude Opus 5.5 through the Anthropic API, with adaptive thinking and per-step effort levels
specs.Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Zod, Anthropic SDK, PyMuPDF, pptxgenjs, docx, resvg (WebAssembly), Tailwind
specs.Hosting: Cloudflare Workers, D1 database, Cloudflare Workflows for background jobs, behind a password

hero.alt: The home screen of the app: a box asking "What are we teaching?" with a Create button, a library of saved lessons and tests below it, and the textbook chapter list down the right side

intake.question: What number can you put on it?
What did you decide, and what did you reject?

intro: Teachers spend hours turning a textbook chapter into a lesson. Lesson Desk does it from one sentence. I built it for my dad, who teaches astronomy and physics, and it is used for both courses. The app itself is named All of a Sutton, which is the name in the screenshots.

It reads the request, picks the chapters and writes a lesson plan. Then it writes the slides, a hands-on group activity and a worksheet in parallel from that plan. All of it is grounded in the class's actual textbook, with page citations in the answer key. Slides reuse figures cropped from the book, or diagrams the model draws itself as SVG. It also builds tests in two shuffled versions and makes balanced student groups.
This is LLM application engineering. I did not train or fine-tune a model. The work is what sits around the model: grounding, structured output, validation, cost and long-running jobs.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: One sentence in, a full class out
body: A 90-minute class needs slides, an activity, a worksheet and an answer key, and they all have to teach the same thing. Building that from a chapter by hand takes hours.
Here the teacher types one sentence, like "make me a lesson on chapter 11". About five minutes later the whole class is ready to open as PowerPoint and Word files.

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.title: How it works
body: A lesson is 5 model calls. One reads the request, one writes the plan, and three write the slides, the activity and the worksheet at the same time. Nothing the model returns is used until it has passed three checks.

flow.summary: The textbooks are split into chapter text and a figure index ahead of time. A teacher request goes to an interpret call, then a plan call, then three parallel calls for slides, activity and worksheet. The results pass a schema check, a figure id check and an SVG safety check, are saved as JSON, and are shown in the browser and exported as PowerPoint and Word files.

sections.label: Grounding
sections.title: Grounded in the textbook, with a figure catalog
body: The model never works from memory. A Python script splits each textbook PDF into chapters using its bookmarks. A second script finds every caption, such as "Figure 11.3", grows a crop outward from it to the nearby graphics, and throws away crops that caught body text.
Each request sends the model the chapter text plus a catalog of that chapter's figures: id, page and caption. The model picks figures by id, and it cites printed page numbers in the answer keys.

sections.label: Plan first
sections.title: Plan first, then fan out
body: One call writes a lesson plan. Three parallel calls then write the slides, the activity and the worksheet, and each one is given the same plan as a blueprint. That is why the three pieces teach the same objectives instead of drifting apart, and why a lesson takes five minutes rather than fifteen.
A cheap, low-effort call at the front routes the request: lesson or test, and which chapters. When it cannot tell, it asks a clarifying question instead of guessing.

sections.label: Structured output
sections.title: Structured output, validated twice
body: Every call returns JSON constrained by a Zod schema, and then I parse it again on my side. The model's answer is data, not prose: slides, questions, answers, points. So the same result renders in the browser and exports to PowerPoint and Word.

sections.label: Validation
sections.title: Never trust model output
body: The model can name a figure that does not exist, or write an SVG that is unsafe. Figure ids are checked against the index. SVG diagrams are rejected if they contain scripts, event handlers, external links or foreignObject. A bad visual is dropped from that one slide rather than failing the deck.
Refusals, cut-off responses, rate limits and bad keys each turn into a message a teacher can act on.

sections.label: Diagrams
sections.title: The model draws its own diagrams
body: When no textbook figure fits, the model writes a diagram as SVG: a force diagram, a graph sketch. The app rasterises it to PNG with resvg compiled to WebAssembly, so it can go into a PowerPoint file.
The first pair below is the same slide in the app and in the exported deck. The rest are more diagrams the model drew for the same physics lesson.

sections.label: Long jobs
sections.title: Long jobs that survive
body: A lesson takes minutes, which is longer than a web request. Hosted, each lesson is a Cloudflare Workflow with one durable step per part, so a failed part can be retried alone and the teacher watches the steps complete.
The teacher can also revise one part, for example "make the worksheet easier", without regenerating the rest.

sections.label: Right tool
sections.title: Not everything needs an LLM
body: Student names are never sent to the model. Grouping is ordinary code: a randomised search of 400 attempts, scored by penalties for keep-apart pairs, repeated past pairings and an uneven ability mix.
Test version B is a seeded shuffle, so it is identical every time it is downloaded.

images.alt: The students and groups screen: a demo roster split into four balanced groups, with controls for students per group and how to mix them
images.caption: Balanced groups in one click. The names are a made-up demo roster of famous scientists, not real students.

facts.Pipeline: 5 model calls per lesson: interpret, plan, then slides, activity and worksheet in parallel
facts.Real run, Astronomy ch. 11: 5 min 23 s, about $2, 55,374 output tokens, 18 slides (9 textbook figures, 5 model-drawn diagrams)
facts.Real run, Physics ch. 4: 3 min 19 s, 39,210 output tokens, 18 slides (10 textbook figures, 6 model-drawn diagrams)
facts.Textbook corpus: 2 books, 64 chapters, 1,119 figures cropped and indexed automatically (465 astronomy, 654 physics)
facts.Code: About 5,000 lines of TypeScript (Next.js 16, React 19) and Python (PDF processing)

sections.label: Next
sections.title: What I learned, and what is next
body: Every call records input, output and cache tokens against the lesson. That telemetry showed the prompt cache was being written but never read: 0 cache-read tokens across the four calls. The likely cause is that each call sends a different output schema. Fixing it should save about $0.50 of the roughly $2 a lesson costs.
After that: a question bank that reuses questions across tests, and recovering the figures the cropper currently discards.

sections.label: Links
body: The repo is private. The live app sits behind a password because it holds licensed textbook content and class rosters, so there is no public link. I can give a demo on request.
